more.question: N3
more.good_when: An accountant reading from the top already knows that invoicer is a command they run by the time KR2.1 speaks of "the command" not running. The document tells them this before KR2.1, so they never have to read ahead to the Concept section to learn what that command is.

more.question: N4
more.good_when: The accounting team and the maintainers see at once how all four key results rank, from first to last. For any change, they can tell which key results come before the one it improves and so must not get worse. Today the text names only KR1.1 and KR2.1 as first and leaves them to guess where KR1.2 and KR2.2 stand.

more.question: N5
more.good_when: Each sentence tells the accountant or the maintainer one thing, says who acts, and reads only one way, in the original or through a machine translation. Several sentences now join two points: the priority rule after its colon, the reason key results have no targets, and the Concept lines on what the accountant and the installer each skip and on what happens when a line is unreadable. The priority sentence also pairs a plural subject with "comes", so a reader stops to work out whether one or both key results are meant.

more.question: N6
more.good_when: The accountant reads the words they use at work. invoicer "prints" their invoice, where the text now says it "returns" the invoice and speaks of "the print". The accountant knows that O1 and KR1.1 stand for an objective and a key result without having to work that out from the heading. Goodhart's law comes with a plain explanation, so no reader needs to know the name already. The maintainers find their own role under the name they use for themselves.
